# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review of the two-year follow-up (Varden County trial and Halden subset)

This report answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents, and largely in the way the evidence pointed:

- the per-hour gain in case-processing persists at 24 months, smaller than at nine months;
- the registered mediation test supports meetings over fatigue;
- the counter arm proved unsustainable;
- the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies.

The authors are measured in tone and candid about the limits of the meeting-audit and Halden data.

There are, however, three substantive problems:

1. The hours figures do not reconcile with the stated definition of log time. This matters because log time is the denominator for the headline estimate and the mediation test.
2. Control offices were contaminated by the meeting audit, which confounds the decay estimate.
3. The mediation result is described as "confirmed" although it rests on the same 14 offices that generated the hypothesis.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Paper | Recomputed | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | +9.8% | 0.966/0.88 = 1.098 | ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months | +8.5% | 0.966/0.89 = 1.085 | ✓ |
| Halden 11 continuers, hours | −13.4% | 34.9/40.3 = 0.866 | ✓ |
| Halden 11, per actual hour | +11.8% | 96.8/86.6 = 1.118 | ✓ |
| Staff needed to restore counter service | 12% | 1/0.886 = +12.9% from the 9-month estimate | ✓ roughly |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | = 100% | ✓ |
| "Declined by about a quarter" | — | 12.5 → 9.8 = −22% (like-for-like) | ✓ |

The calculations are right. The problems are in how the figures fit together.

---

## 1. The log-hours measure doesn't reconcile with the other hours figures

Log time is defined as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system", i.e. time working on cases. On that definition it excludes meetings. Combining the paper's own figures:

- **Meetings:** relative to control, fell by about 3.3 hours per week (treated 7.4 → 3.9; control 7.2 → 7.0).
- **Timesheet hours:** fell 12% relative to control. From a baseline of about 37.9 hours, that is roughly 4.5 hours.
- **Implied non-meeting work:** therefore fell by only about 1.2 hours, roughly 4% of about 30.5 hours.
- **Log hours:** reportedly fell 11%. If they measure casework, they should have fallen about 4%.

For log time to fall 11% while meetings fell 3.3 hours, total hours would have had to fall about 18%, not 12%. Something here is inconsistent. Possible explanations include log time capturing only part of casework, or log time including periods spent in meetings while logged in. The authors should report levels in hours for timesheets, logs and meetings in both arms, not just percentage changes.

This is not a minor point, because it changes what the mediation result means.

- **If log time excludes meetings,** cutting meetings cannot raise output per log-hour by removing low-value time from the denominator. It would have to work some other way, for example through fewer interruptions and longer blocks of focused casework. That is a plausible mechanism, but a different one from "removing low-value time", which is how the nine-month report framed it.
- **If log time includes meetings,** the description in Section 2 is wrong.

The authors need to say which applies.

Relatedly, logs were "added" at follow-up and Table 1 shows no nine-month log figure. A difference-in-differences estimate needs pre-period log data. Presumably the system holds historical logs, but the report should say so.

## 2. Control contamination confounds the decay estimate

The month-15 meeting audit in two control offices is contamination, not just an "unplanned observation". Those offices raised their output per hour by 4.1%. If the seven control offices are of similar size, that alone lifts the control mean by about 1.2 percentage points and mechanically lowers the treated-minus-control estimate.

So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect controls improving rather than the treatment effect fading. Perhaps a third of the 2.7-point decline could come from this. The authors should:

- report the 24-month estimate excluding the two audit offices, as a sensitivity analysis;
- say whether the audit was prompted by knowledge of the trial's nine-month findings, which seems likely.

There are two further problems with the decay claim.

- **The Summary compares unlike measures.** It reports a fall "from 12.5% to 8.5%", which compares the timesheet measure at nine months with the log measure at 24 months. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, as the body of the report correctly states. The Summary overstates the decline.
- **The decline is not tested.** The intervals (6.9 to 18.4 and 4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "Declined by about a quarter", stated as a finding in Section 5, needs a test of the difference between the two time points.

There is also an unexplained arithmetic tension. If two of the seven control offices cut meetings by 2.1 hours, the control average should fall by about 0.6 hours. It fell by only 0.2 hours (7.2 → 7.0), implying the other five control offices increased their meeting time. That may be true, but it should be shown.

## 3. The mediation result is supportive, not confirmatory

The registered protocol is a real improvement, but "confirms" in the Summary overstates what this analysis can establish.

- **Same offices.** The hypothesis came from the seven treated offices (r = 0.71 at month six), and the test uses the same seven offices. It is a pre-specified test on extended data from the same units, not an independent replication. Registration at month 11 also came after the meetings association had been seen.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated observations, not independent information about differences between offices. With 14 clusters, an interval of 28% to 66% looks narrower than I would expect. The authors should state how clustering was handled and whether a small-cluster correction was used. This is the same issue I raised about the nine-month report, and it is still not addressed for any estimate.
- **Assumptions.** The Limitations section acknowledges the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. A further issue is that the two mediators are likely linked: fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. The 47% and 18% shares are not cleanly additive, and they depend on how the joint model is specified.
- **Where the baseline meeting data came from.** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. If these were recovered retrospectively from calendar systems, the report should say so and describe how complete the records are.

Read appropriately, the result is still informative. Meetings account for roughly 4 percentage points of the 8.5% gain, fatigue for about 1.5 points, and about 3 points are unexplained. The registered test consistently favours meetings over fatigue as a pathway. I would describe that as supporting the meetings hypothesis, not confirming it.

## 4. The meeting audit is more suggestive than the authors say

The two audit offices cut meetings by 2.1 hours and gained 4.1%, about 2 percentage points per hour of meetings removed. The treated arm's meetings pathway gives about 4.0 points for about 3.3 hours cut, roughly 1.2 points per hour.

On this crude comparison, reorganising alone yielded at least as much per meeting-hour as reorganising alongside reduced hours. With n = 2 and a before-after comparison, this proves nothing. Seasonality and regression to the mean are both plausible explanations. But it points away from "the hours cut is what makes reorganisation happen", at least for the reorganisation itself.

The authors already have a better comparison available. They could compare the two audit offices with the other five control offices over the same months. That would remove the seasonality problem from the "own previous six months" comparison.

The closing point, that no arm reorganised without reducing hours, is exactly right. A three-arm trial would settle it: reduced hours, meeting reorganisation alone, and control.

## 5. The Halden subset

- **The baseline looks borrowed.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the figure Varga & Holm reported for the 27 time-tracking organisations, not these 11. If the 11 were measured against another group's baseline, the +11.8% is not valid. The authors should confirm that the 11 used their own baselines, and say how many of the 11 actually had time tracking.
- **Selection is compounded.** 14 of 23 organisations responded (61%), and non-responders plausibly include organisations that did poorly. The "survivors twice over" framing is honest. "Upper bound" is slightly too strong, since unlogged day-off work could still inflate the estimate, but the intent is right.
- **The figure does not show durability.** The +11.8% at 24 months is similar to the +10.8% at six months in the 17-organisation subset. But these are different subsets, and the continuers are selected on success, so this cannot show that gains persist.
- **New information.** A marketing agency, a discretionary-work setting, reverted citing client deadlines, with output at reversion of 88–91. Some client-facing discretionary work evidently behaves more like coverage-bound work. That is worth noting in light of the meta-analysis's binary coding of work type, which its own Limitations already flagged.

## 6. Matters left unaddressed

- **Halden's attrition misdescription.** A Halden author (Okafor) co-authors this report, but it does not respond to Varga & Holm's finding that seven of the nine withdrawals came after the reduced schedule began. This was the natural place to correct or contest it.
- **Backlogs and deadlines.** Two years is enough time for backlogs to build or for statutory deadlines to be breached. Neither is reported, although both were identified as risks in the nine-month Limitations.
- **Cost in case-processing.** The report estimates cost per contact for the counter arm (+9%) but not cost per case for case-processing. With full pay, overtime, and output per employee at −3.4%, cost per case almost certainly rose. This remains the main gap across all five documents.
- **Sick days.** The −27% figure still isn't adjusted for scheduled days.
- **Uncertainty.** Resignations and appeal-overturn rates still have no confidence intervals. The output-per-employee interval (−8.0 to +1.2) admits a loss of up to 8%. "Mostly, not fully, offset" is fair, but readers should be told the lower bound.
- **Possible conflict of interest.** The authors are adjudicating claims about their own earlier hypothesis and their critics. They do so fairly, but phrases such as "since dismissed as post hoc" and "survives" carry some advocacy. Neutral wording would serve them better.

## 7. Section 5 is largely right

- **On the re-analysis:** an 8.5% gain under randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon does refute "entirely an artifact". This is subject to the log-hours question in point 1 and the small-cluster inference issue. Continuous evaluation over 24 months still leaves a residual Hawthorne effect possible, but a pure novelty explanation is now hard to sustain.
- **On the meta-analysis:** the revelation that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms that the "no decay" claim cannot stand. The meta-analysis should be corrected. One trial of 14 offices is, however, also a thin basis for "declined by about a quarter" as a general finding.

---

## Suggested revisions

1. Reconcile the hours measures. Report levels for timesheets, logs and meetings by arm, and define precisely what log time includes.
2. Clarify the mediation mechanism in light of point 1: denominator effect or focus effect.
3. Use like-for-like figures (12.5% → 9.8%) in the Summary, and test the decline formally.
4. Report the 24-month estimate excluding the two audit offices, and compare the audit offices with the other control offices.
5. Change "confirms" to "supports". State the clustering and small-cluster method used for all intervals.
6. Document where the baseline meeting data came from.
7. Confirm the baseline used for the 11 Halden organisations.
8. Add backlog, deadline and cost-per-case outcomes for case-processing.
9. Respond to the Halden attrition finding.

---

## Updated evidence summary

| Question | Before this report | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–12% at ≤9 months | About 8.5–10% at 24 months in one randomised trial; possibly understated by control contamination |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | 0 to −3% | About −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) |
| Coverage-bound work | About −9 to −11% per worker, worse service | Abandoned by the county at month 12; restoring service estimated at +12% staff and +9% cost per contact |
| Durability | Unresolved | Gain persists to 24 months with modest, untested decline |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | Refuted, subject to the log-hours query |
| "No decay" (meta-analysis) | Weakly supported | Unsupported: the four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours |
| Mechanism | Fatigue weak; meetings untested | Meetings favoured over fatigue in a registered test on the same offices; about a third unexplained |
| Gains without cutting hours? | Untested | Two-office audit suggests possibly; needs a three-arm trial |
| Cost per unit of output | Unreported | Reported for counters only; still missing for discretionary work |

The research priorities are now fairly clear:

1. A trial with a reorganisation-only arm.
2. Cost-per-output measures.
3. Independent replication outside a single public employer.

I can draft a consolidated brief across all five documents if that would help.
